activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number makes an equivalent fraction, so one quarter equals three twelfths.
story:
Hunter stared at the whiteboard like it had insulted him personally. "One quarter plus one third." He read it out loud in the voice people use for curses. "You can't even add those. They don't match."

"Ms. Anderson says we have to justify every step," said Delia, sliding into the seat beside him. The classroom smelled like pencil shavings and the lemon cleaner the janitor used, and someone's leftover pizza sat in a box on the back table from the lunch club, cold and sad.

"So justify this: it's impossible."

Delia grabbed a paper towel and went to the pizza box. She tore one big quarter slice free, then cut a remaining quarter into three thin strips. "Watch. One quarter," she said, holding up the big piece. Then she laid the three little strips side by side where the big one had been. They covered exactly the same space. "One quarter equals three twelfths. Cutting it into more slices doesn't change how much pizza there is."

Hunter squinted at the greasy towel. "So if I multiply the top and the bottom of one quarter by three, I get three twelfths, and it's still the same amount?"

"Now you're dangerous."

He grabbed his pencil and worked fast. One quarter became three twelfths. One third became four twelfths. He added them and got seven twelfths, then checked it against the pizza, counting ragged pieces of pepperoni like a tiny accountant. It held.

"Okay, but what about subtracting?" he said. "Five sixths minus one half." He tested his new idea the same way, multiplying one half's top and bottom by three to get three sixths, then taking it away. Two sixths. He looked at the paper towel again and cut a slice into six pieces to check, and the pieces covered the same space as before, which felt almost like a magic trick that wasn't cheating.

Cain wandered over from the window, where he'd been watching a squirrel stage a heist on the vending machine. "Hunter doing math voluntarily?" he said. "I need to sit down. Is this legitimate? Did someone swap his brain?"

"My brain is fine. My brain now understands common denominators." Hunter held up the paper towel like a trophy. "Also, that pizza is a legitimate teaching tool, so back off."

"Then it deserves a prescription," said Cain, writing on a sticky note: eat more pizza, twice daily, for math health. He slapped it on Hunter's desk.

Ms. Anderson collected the towels and Hunter's crumpled worksheet, and paused at the seven twelfths circled twice. "Nice work," she said. "Though next time, maybe use paper."

Hunter looked at the pizza box. "Paper doesn't smell this good."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil that producers use again.
story:
Peyton had drawn her food chain four times, and every time Ms. Johansson walked past without stopping. Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk. It was neat. It had arrows. It was correct, Peyton was almost sure, and yet something felt unfinished, like a puzzle missing a piece she could not see.

"You should put it on the big paper," Madisyn whispered, sliding the poster board across the table. "I want mine up on the wall by Friday, and if yours is better, there's only room for one." Madisyn had already outlined hers in three colors. Peyton looked at her own hawk, the top predator, circling at the top of the page, then at the empty corner below the grass where she had smudged out a mistake. Marcel leaned over from the next seat.

"Ms. Johansson said the best one explains what happens when a link disappears," he said. "Like if the frogs all got sick. Then the snakes go hungry, and the grasshoppers go wild and eat everything." He tapped the empty corner. "But she also said there's a link almost everybody forgets."

Peyton's pencil stopped. She raised her hand. "If the hawk dies, where does it go? It just... disappears?" Ms. Johansson smiled but did not answer, which meant Peyton had to figure it out herself. She remembered the science table by the window, where the class had set an old log from the nature walk. On its underside, small pale mushrooms had pushed up through the soft wood. Peyton had thought they were just decoration. Now she got up, walked over, and turned the log carefully.

"Madisyn, look," she said. "Fungi. They break down the dead plants and animals and return the nutrients to the soil, and then the grass uses them again." She hurried back and drew the mushrooms in the empty corner, arrows looping from the hawk and the dead grass back down to the soil and up to the sun again. "Consumers eat, but these guys clean up. Without them, the whole chain would run out." Madisyn frowned at her own flat, one-way poster, then grabbed a fresh pencil. "Okay," she muttered, "but I'm still drawing mine bigger."

"Raccoons are tough," Marcel offered, "but a hawk with no snakes is pretty vulnerable."

Ms. Johansson stopped at their table and pinned Peyton's poster to the wall.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like honey cake, which Victor thought was a strange thing to bake right before nobody was allowed to eat. "So it's not just till sundown tomorrow?" he asked, because that was what he had assumed all year at home.

"No," Grandpa said, checking the clock even though the sun was still up. "The Yom Kippur fast lasts about twenty-five hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next. Three stars, roughly." He said it the way he said the weather report, not like a lesson.

Victor had eaten breakfast at seven, lunch at noon, and a big plate of pasta at five, thinking he was being clever. Now he did the math on his fingers. If the fast started at sunset tonight, around six forty, and went until after nightfall tomorrow, past seven, he would go more than a full day with nothing. He hadn't prepared for that. He wasn't even sure he wanted to do it, but he'd told Brendan on Friday that it was mandatory for him this year, and Brendan had said, "Isn't that just a stereotype, that every Jewish kid fasts?" Victor had said no, his family really did it, and he'd wanted to prove he could too.

At eight that night his stomach growled so loudly that Grandpa raised an eyebrow from his armchair. Victor drank a cup of water, since water was allowed in Grandpa's version, and worked out a theory. His hunger came in waves, he noticed, so if he lay down during a wave instead of pacing the hallway, maybe the wave would pass without him noticing. It was like the time he'd waited out a cramp during a swim meet instead of getting out of the pool. He tested it, lying on the guest bed with his hands folded, and the wave did pass, which felt like a small secret about something he couldn't see.

The twist came at noon the next day, when the phone rang and it was Brendan, asking how long the fast really was. "I thought you'd quit by morning," Brendan admitted. "I kind of hoped you would, honestly, so I wouldn't have to apologize for laughing." Victor sat on the porch steps, watching the sky and thinking about how he'd almost quit too, about the granola bar he'd taken out of the pantry and then put back. He wondered whether putting it back counted as strength or whether he was just afraid to compromise in front of Grandpa. He told Brendan the truth, all twenty-five hours of it, sunset to after nightfall.

"You're still going?" Brendan asked. "It's like four more hours."

"I'm still going," Victor said, and hung up, and went back inside to find the honey cake.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
Luke's grandfather had cleared the kitchen table and covered it with a purple cloth, and now he was standing in front of it with a shoebox full of photographs, doing nothing. Luke counted to thirty before he said anything.

"Grandma Vega's side of the family," his grandfather said finally. "They always did this. First and second of November." He lifted out a photo of Grandma at about twenty, laughing on a bicycle. "We set the photo out with marigolds. The color and the scent are supposed to guide the spirit home."

"So it's like a landing beacon," Luke said.

"An ofrenda," his grandfather said. "That's what they call the altar."

Luke took the shoebox to the table and began arranging things with his usual approach, which was to put them down fast. Keira, who had come over because she was helping him sort the garage and refused to leave a job unfinished, took one look and pulled the photo back out.

"You're putting her where people will knock her over with their elbows," Keira said. "Center. Slightly raised." She had been meticulous about the garage too, labeling boxes with a pen she carried for that purpose. Her real goal, Luke suspected, was to be the one who got the photo angle exactly right, and she adjusted it three times.

The marigolds were the problem. They had a whole bundle from the flower stand, but Luke got to wondering. If the scent was the guide, then one vase wasn't really a path. He tried a test: he scattered petals in a line from the front door, down the hall, to the table, then stood at the door and sniffed his way along it. He could smell each cluster, faint but there, all the way to the photo. It worked. It probably worked. There was no way to check the part that mattered, which was the part he could not see, and he decided that was fine, because Grandma had never needed a map to find anything in this house, including the cookies he hid.

Warren arrived with his dad's casserole, looked at the petal trail, and said it was a fire hazard. "It's an adaptation," Luke told him. "The flowers adapted to the floor." Warren changed his mind when he walked the trail and admitted the smell was incredible, like citrus and dirt in a good way, and then he took over handing petals to Keira, who prescribed an even spacing between them, two fingers wide, no clumps.

At dusk they lit the candles. Luke's grandfather set the casserole on the table too, because Grandma would have wanted dinner first, and they all stood in the doorway where the trail began.

"Door's open," Luke's grandfather said, and he left it open.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
Levi had been counting the granola bars in the pantry for three days, and every morning there was one fewer. Nobody in his house admitted to taking them. His sister Mara rolled her eyes whenever he asked, and his dad just shrugged and said maybe Levi was miscounting, though Levi knew he was not.

On Saturday his friend Ruth came over to work on their science homework, and Levi told her about the disappearing bars. "Mr. Sato would say you need a hypothesis," she said, poking through the pantry. "That's a testable guess. Like, maybe Mara is taking them, and you could set up a camera." Levi frowned. "My dad kept saying, 'My theory is you're sleepwalking and eating them yourself.' But that's not a theory, is it? Mr. Sato drilled that into us last week." Ruth nodded. "Right. A theory is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported. A hypothesis is an idea still being tested." Levi pulled out his notebook. "So I have three hypotheses. Mara, me, or the dog. And I'm going to test all of them."

The test took some planning, and Ruth insisted on helping, which meant Levi had an obligation to share whatever granola bars survived. He spread flour thinly across the pantry floor before bed, a trick he'd read about for tracking footprints, though he had to accommodate the dog by shutting her out of the kitchen entirely so she couldn't wander through and ruin the evidence. The flour made the dark floor look faintly pale, like frost.

In the morning the pantry door stood open, and Levi crouched over the flour with his heart pounding. There were no dog prints. There were no big sneaker prints either. There was a trail of small bare footprints, heel to toe, walking in, and walking out, and they stopped halfway across the kitchen. He followed them with Ruth behind him, holding her breath. The trail ended at the hallway closet, where the door was shut but not latched. Levi swung it open and found Mara sitting on the floor with crumbs on her chin and the last granola bar half unwrapped in her fist.

"You said you weren't eating them," Levi said.

"I said I wasn't stealing them," Mara answered. "I was sleepwalking. Probably."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
The argument started over a half-eaten pretzel at lunch. Steven said most students at their school walked to school, and Gavin said that was ridiculous, because the bike racks were always packed. "That's just your opinion," Steven said, mouth full. "It's not an opinion, it's a fact," Gavin shot back, and then neither of them could explain the difference, which was annoying. Adrien, who was drawing in the margins of his science notebook, looked up and said they should just count.

Gavin thought about the time in fourth grade when he had sworn the gym was bigger than the cafeteria and Ms. Popescu had let the class measure both with a tape reel. The gym was shorter by four feet. He had been so sure, and so wrong, and he still remembered the squeak of the tape and the smell of floor wax. "Fine," he said now. "We check it."

In Ms. Popescu's room, the poster wall was sparse, just a periodic table and a sign-up sheet, so there was room to tape up a blank chart titled HOW WE GET TO SCHOOL. Gavin had written his plan on a notecard the night before: two counters at the front doors, two at the side gate, tally marks for walkers, bikes, buses, and cars. He had wanted to postpone the whole thing until Monday, but Adrien pointed out that Friday counts just as well as any other day. At 7:50 they took their positions. The morning smelled like rain on asphalt, and the tally marks piled up faster than Gavin expected. He kept losing count whenever someone shouted hello.

By first bell the chart showed something Gavin had not predicted. Walkers outnumbered everything else combined, even though the bike racks, which he could see from the doorway, looked like a jungle of handlebars. Only nine bikes, but forty-one pairs of feet, plus the bus kids and a slow parade of minivans.

"Most students at our school walk to school," Adrien read off the chart. "Nobody had checked it before today, and it still could have been checked. That's the difference. It was checkable the whole time." Steven chewed his pretzel and studied the tallies like they might rearrange themselves.

"So what was my opinion, then?" Gavin asked.

"That the bike racks matter," Steven said. "That one you can't count."

Gavin looked out the window at the racks, gleaming and crowded, then back at the forty-one tally marks. He picked up the marker and, under the chart, wrote DO BIKES FEEL LOUDER BECAUSE THEY'RE SHINY? A girl passing in the hall stopped, read it, and laughed all the way to class.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
The neighborhood cleanup ended at the community center, where a folding table held boxes of slightly bruised apples, crooked carrots and one bizarre potato shaped like a duck. Emily had signed up for the food bank shift thinking she would sort cans, but the produce had come from somewhere, and nobody could tell her where. "Mr. Hussain's orchard, mostly," said Maxime, stacking apples. "And the garden plots behind Rowan's building. But the boxes keep arriving all afternoon." Emily noticed a pattern: each box had a torn scrap of paper taped to it, and each scrap was in the same handwriting, small and slanted. She decided to test whether one person was behind all of it, and dug through the boxes to excavate every last note.

The notes did not say much. "Take these," said one. "They are fine," said another. But the seventh note, stuck to the duck potato, was longer, and Emily read it out loud. "Dear volunteers. You would not know me. In the old story from the Book of Leviticus, farmers are told to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers. My granddaughter calls this gleaning. I leave my edges. Please use them. Signed, E. Bramble." Rowan squinted at it. "So somebody is leaving the edges of their garden on purpose?" "That's the rule," Emily said. "The unharvested edges are for people who need food. And strangers."

Mr. Hussain came in carrying yet another box, and Emily held up the notes like evidence. "Verdict?" he said, setting it down. "We think one woman, E. Bramble, is behind everything, including the duck potato." He laughed. "Mrs. Bramble is eighty-four. She's been leaving her garden edges for years, and she told me once she got the idea from that old story. Nobody ever caught her because she drops the boxes and hurries off."

The twist, when it came, arrived with the last box of the day. Taped inside was a fresh note. "I saw the girl sorting my carrots. Next Saturday I will leave the front edge too. Tell her the potato is a duck." Emily put it in her pocket, and the potato, carefully, on the shelf where everyone could see it.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: Many Canadian municipalities let residents ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting, which is called appearing as a delegation.
story:
Emmett stood on Grandma's back porch with his speech cards, shuffling them like a card trick he hadn't learned yet. Tomorrow night he had five minutes in front of the city council to argue that the bylaw banning skateboards from Founders Plaza should be changed, and so far his opening line was "Hi, I'm Emmett," followed by a very long silence.

"Hold this," Grandma said, pressing a purple lump into his free hand. She was making a flamingo out of polymer clay for the garden club contest on Saturday, and its neck kept drooping. "If I win, I get the blue ribbon and bragging rights over Mr. Smith's rooster. Now give. Let's hear the speech."

He read it out loud, flat as a workbook page, and Grandma winced. The problem, Emmett realized, went back to April, when he'd mailed a letter about the plaza and gotten nothing but a form reply saying the matter was noted. Noted. He'd wondered for weeks whether anyone at City Hall actually read letters, or whether they fell into some deep drawer that could generate silence forever. Maybe the problem wasn't his argument. Maybe it was the channel it traveled through.

"Grandma," he said slowly, "if I sent a letter and nothing happened, what if there's a way to get in the room? Like, in person?"

She tapped her rolling pin against the table. "There is. Many municipalities let residents ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting. It's called appearing as a delegation. Your grandfather did it once about the garbage schedule."

Emmett felt the pieces click. A letter was a message in a bottle. A delegation was a handshake. He called the clerk's office from the kitchen phone, wrote down what to do, and got a spot on tomorrow's agenda. Then he rebuilt his speech. Instead of paragraphs, he tried three claims: the plaza's smooth stone was built for rolling, the ban pushed skaters onto the sidewalk where collisions were more likely, and a trial hour on Sunday mornings could test it. He tested the speech on Grandma's garden gnome, on Grandma, and finally on Lilith and Kaya, who biked over after dinner and sat on the lush grass by her tomato beds, firing questions at him like a real council might.

"Why should we risk it?" Kaya demanded, playing a difficult councillor.

"Because right now the bylaw generates the exact problem it was supposed to prevent," Emmett said. "Skaters don't disappear. They move somewhere worse."

On Saturday morning, Grandma set her finished flamingo on the porch rail, its neck held straight by a hidden wire. Emmett drove with her to City Hall, cards in his pocket, and when his name was called he walked to the microphone. "Hi, I'm Emmett," he said, and this time the words kept coming.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking a government body to take a specific action.
story:
Jaxson stood on the wide marble steps of city hall with a clipboard under his arm and a knot in his stomach. Behind him, Celia counted the signature pages for the third time. "Forty-one," she said. "The same as the last two times."

"Forty-one out of how many houses?" Aria asked, hopping down one step at a time.

"Ninety-something," Celia said. "Half the street didn't answer, and Mr. Pell slammed his door so fast I still feel the wind."

Jaxson looked up at the tall doors. Last month, Milo from his class had been hit by a car at the corner of Fern and Second, right where they all crossed to get to school. He was okay now, mostly, but nobody walked there without looking four times. Jaxson had asked his dad why there was no crosswalk, and his dad had said, "City things don't change because one person asks. They change because a lot of people ask at the same time, in writing." That idea had stuck in Jaxson's head like a song he couldn't shake. One voice was too quiet. So he had tested it. He had written down exactly what they wanted, a painted crosswalk with a crossing guard at Fern and Second, and gone door to door asking people to sign their names under it.

Inside, they followed the signs to the clerk's office. A woman behind the counter peered at them through translucent reading glasses that made her eyes look larger and softer than they probably were. "Can I help you?"

"We want to give this to a councillor," Jaxson said, and slid the pages across. "It's a petition. It's a written request, signed by a lot of people, asking the city to take a specific action."

The clerk smiled at that, like he'd said a magic word correctly. "Then you take it to the councillor's office, room 204, and you can ask to speak at the next council meeting." She stamped the front page. "You'll need to fill in a form, and you might want more signatures. Forty-one is a start, though."

On the way to room 204, Aria whispered, "So we're not done?"

"We're not done," Jaxson said. "But look." The stamp on the page said RECEIVED, in blue ink, right under forty-one names.

Celia grinned. "Mr. Pell is going to sign next time. I'm bringing cookies."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races because it is the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes.
story:
Luca stood at the shallow end of the backyard pool and counted the plastic flags Mr. Mokoena had strung along the fence. Twenty-five metres, his dad had measured, exactly the length of a real race pool. Last week Luca had promised his friends he would swim the whole way front crawl, with side breathing, before Saturday. So far he had made it twelve metres before coughing, standing up, and retrieving his goggles from the bottom of the drain.

"You're turning your whole face up," said Haris, who was sitting on the wall with his feet in the water. "My cousin does it sideways, like she's resting her ear on the water."

Luca tried resting his ear on the water. He swallowed less, but he still ran out of air halfway. He floated on his back and stared at the flags, wondering. Why did swimmers even bother with this stroke? When they had watched the freestyle race on television, every single lane had used the same arm-winding style, none of them doing breaststroke or backstroke. "Freestyle means you can pick any stroke you want," Haris said, dangling his toes. "So why does everyone pick the same one?"

Luca chewed on that. Maybe the answer was the same reason a lemonade stand made more income when it sold cold drinks on the hottest day: people choose whatever works best. If every swimmer in the race, from every country, all chose front crawl, then front crawl had to be the fastest of the competitive strokes. That felt credible to him, like something you could trust because so many people kept proving it. But if it was the fastest, the problem wasn't the stroke. The problem had to be his breathing.

He had been assuming he needed a breath every two strokes because his body felt desperate. Maybe the desperate feeling came first from splashing, not from real tiredness. He tested it: one slow lap, arms easy, kicking calm, face down until his cheek barely broke the surface, then a small sideways sip of air. No splash in his mouth. He tried again with three strokes between breaths, then five. The water hissed past his ears and the flags slid overhead one after another.

The wall of the deep end bumped his fingertips. He stood up, gasping and grinning, and pushed his goggles up onto his forehead. "Twenty-five metres," he said. "Count the flags if you don't believe me."

"I believe you," Haris said, and jumped in to try it himself.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:43 on Tuesday night, right after Colton finished the dishes. Wade had posted a photo of the half-built skate park behind the middle school, with the caption: "they're wasting two million dollars on this dump, my uncle says it'll be dead in a month."

Van replied first, three crying-laughing faces, then "rip our tax dollars." Colton started to type "yeah total waste" and stopped, because at dinner his dad had done a thing with a letter to the local paper. The letter said almost the same words, and his dad had tapped it with one finger and said, "Two million dollars, I can check that. Whether it's a waste, that's just the writer talking." His mom had put the letter under the fruit bowl, which in their house meant the discussion was over.

Colton deleted his reply. He typed instead: "the two million part is checkable. the waste part is just a feeling." Then he sat there wondering if that sounded like something a dad would say.

"checkable how," Wade wrote back.

Colton went looking. The town's website had a page about the project, and after some digging he found the actual number in the meeting minutes. The park did cost two million dollars. That part of Wade's sentence was true, which felt strange, because Wade's uncle had still said it like it proved something. It proved the number and nothing else. Colton pasted the link into the chat and added, "so half your sentence has a citation and half of it doesn't."

Van sent a single question mark, so Colton explained the way he could, without using his dad's exact words, since those were under the fruit bowl now. "like, that sentence is two different kinds of sentence glued together. the cost can be checked. 'a waste' can't. they're distinct things even though they're in one line."

There was a long pause, long enough that Colton could hear the dishwasher running in the kitchen. Then Wade wrote, "ok but is it a dump though." Colton looked at the photo again. The concrete was poured, the ramps weren't installed yet, and there was a mountain of gravel with a porta-potty next to it like a flag planted on the moon. Honestly, at this exact moment, it did look like a dump.

"can't check that from a photo," Colton typed. "go look at it."

The next day after school, Wade and Van were already at the fence when Colton rode up. Wade had his phone out, taking a picture of the same gravel pile from a new angle. "For the chat," he said. "This one's just an opinion, but it's mine."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Gas bubbles that appear when two substances mix, like the fizz when baking soda meets vinegar, are one sign that a chemical change has happened.
story:
The vinegar bottle was almost empty, and Tyler's little sister's volcano was due at her classroom in forty minutes. The volcano itself was robust, built from clay over a soda bottle, with painted ridges and even a tiny plastic rodent frozen mid-scuttle on the slope. The rodent was supposed to look dramatic when the "lava" came. Instead the whole thing sat there doing nothing, because Tyler had used the last of the baking soda on a test run at seven in the morning and had nothing left to prove.

He called Elisa first. She showed up at the kitchen door holding a box of baking soda like it was a rescue supply. "Hunter's coming too," she said. "He wants to see if it explodes."

"It doesn't explode," Tyler said. "It fizzes."

That was the problem, actually. His sister had asked him, last night, watching the test run bubble over the clay, where the bubbles came from. Tyler had opened his mouth and realized he didn't exactly know. He'd said "the volcano does it," which even he could hear was a bad answer. Ms. Carvalho, her teacher, had told the class they had to be able to explain their projects, or no points.

Hunter arrived and read the recipe card taped to the counter. "It says baking soda inside, vinegar on top. So the bubbles come from them mixing."

Tyler set out two cups while the clock on the stove ticked toward departure time. In the first cup he put a spoonful of baking soda and a splash of vinegar. Bubbles rushed up the sides. In the second cup he put a spoonful of sugar, just sugar, and poured the same vinegar over it. Nothing. The sugar sat there. He tried salt next. Still nothing, just wet salt.

"So it's not the vinegar making bubbles by itself," Elisa said, leaning over the counter.

"And it's not fizzing because something melts," Hunter said. He'd grabbed an ice cube from the freezer and was holding it over the warm dish rack, watching it drip. "When ice melts it just goes liquid. No bubbles."

Tyler looked at the cup still fizzing, then at the paper his sister was supposed to read aloud. He picked up the pencil and wrote at the top: Gas bubbles that appear when two substances mix, like the fizz when baking soda meets vinegar, are one sign that a chemical change has happened. Under it he wrote, in smaller letters, melting is only a physical change, and beside that he drew the ice cube with an arrow.

His sister came downstairs in her boots, dragging the volcano by its base, the plastic rodent riding the slope like it was braced for the end of the world. Tyler handed her the paper and the baking soda.

"Where do the bubbles come from?" she asked him again, right there in the kitchen, one more time, as if testing whether he'd earned his twenty minutes of tutoring.

"The fizz when baking soda meets vinegar," Tyler said, "means a chemical change happened. Read your paper."

She read it. In the doorway, Hunter was already making a second cup fizz for no reason except that he could.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
story:
Ellie had been on the couch for three days, watching the steam rise off her mug of tea. The vapor drifted toward the ceiling, and she tracked it with her eyes because there was nothing else to do. The flu had knocked her down one abrupt afternoon, right before the school talent show, and she was missing the rehearsals she was supposed to run with Lisa and Chaya. Her part of the act was the juggling routine, and if she missed too many practices, the whole thing could fall apart.

She found her mother in the kitchen. "Can you call the doctor and ask for antibiotics? Strong ones. If I take them today, I could be back at school by Thursday."

Her mother looked up from chopping an apple. "That's not how it works, but call and ask if you want." She dialed and handed over the phone, and Ellie asked the nurse her question. The answer came back plain and simple: antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, and the flu is a virus, so they would not help her get better even a single day faster.

Ellie hung up slowly. Bacteria and viruses were two different things, and her medicine cabinet was useless against one of them. She sat back on the couch and thought about what a body actually needed to fight a virus, and decided it was the same thing her grandmother was always saying: rest, fluids, and no rushing. To conserve her energy, she canceled everything except sleeping, sipping tea, and one short phone call each evening.

Lisa called that night with a report. "We moved your juggling to the second half so you get more time to heal. Chaya taped the rehearsal on her tablet so you can study it from the couch."

"Send it," Ellie said, and propped the tablet against her pillow, watching the pattern of the pins rise and fall under Lisa's bedroom lamp.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
Samuel laced his cleats so fast he nearly snapped a lace. Today was the first real practice of the season, and Mr. Suryanto had promised something new: tug-of-war to build strength for the soccer team. Emerson had been talking about it all week, mostly because Emerson wanted to be picked as team captain, and captains, he said, always got to stand at the front of the rope.

The grass smelled freshly cut, and the afternoon sun warmed the back of Samuel's neck as Mr. Suryanto dragged a thick rope onto the field. "We'll start with the whole team against me and my spring scale," the coach announced, looping the rope through a handle on a stake he'd hammered into the ground. Eight boys heaved. The scale needle jumped, then sagged. Mr. Suryanto squinted at it, then at them. "Some of you are easing off," he said. Then, almost to himself: "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller."

Samuel couldn't stop thinking about that on the walk home to the basement flat his family rented. He shared the building with a tenant upstairs, a quiet pianist, and her music drifted down through the ceiling while Samuel turned the coach's words over. You couldn't see anyone easing off. It was invisible. So how would anyone know it was real? He decided to infer it the only way he could think of: measure.

At the next practice, Samuel asked Mr. Suryanto to borrow the spring scale. "Let's each pull alone first," he said, holding up a notebook. Zack, the smallest kid on the team, went first and yanked the needle to a number that made Emerson snort. Then they pulled in pairs, then fours, then all eight. Samuel wrote every number down, tongue between his teeth. When he worked out the averages, his pencil nearly tore the page. Alone, each boy pulled harder. Together, every single average had shrunk. Even Zack's. Even his own. "It's true," he whispered. "Everybody does it, not just lazy people. Nobody even notices."

"But we still have to pull together on Saturday," Emerson groaned, and then his face changed, the way it did when he was about to grab at captain things. "Unless we trick ourselves. What if we count? One, two, pull. One, two, pull. Like a drumbeat."

Saturday came with cold wind flapping the corner flags and mud sucking at their shoes. The other team was bigger and louder, and their supporters, including the pianist tenant from upstairs, waved scarves on the sideline. The whistle blew. "One, two, pull!" Emerson bellowed, assertive as a drill sergeant, and eight boys heaved as one. The rope jerked. The red ribbon slid toward them, and Zack, mud-streaked and grinning, drove his heels in and screamed, "PULL!"

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Burning is a chemical change: wood combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and it cannot turn back into wood.
story:
The note landed on Mason's desk during homeroom, folded into a lopsided triangle. He smoothed it flat and read Marina's handwriting: "You were wrong at the campfire. Ice can melt and freeze back because nothing new gets made. I'm proving it in science. Bring the marshmallows." Mason read it twice. He remembered arguing at the cookout that the logs could turn back into wood somehow, if you just added water or waited long enough, and Marina had laughed so hard she nearly dropped her stick.

He brought the marshmallows. Mr. Cardinal set out three stations on the long counter by the window: a bowl of ice cubes, a sealed jar with rusty nails soaking in salty water, and a metal tray holding a splinter of pine. "Transport your notebooks between stations," he said, "and record what you observe." Marina went straight for the jar, because the rust was her proof, and Bryden hovered near the ice, poking a half-melted cube with a pencil until Mr. Cardinal gave him a look.

At the ice station, Mason watched the cubes shrink into puddles, then slid the bowl into the freezer down the hall. When he came back, he held the splinter over the candle Mr. Cardinal had lit for the burning station. The wood caught, flared, and curled into gray flakes and smoke. "So the wood combined with oxygen," Marina said, crowding in beside him, "and it turned into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour." Bryden leaned close. "That's a chemical change," he said. "Like rusting." Mason felt a small sting of resentment that they got to say it first, but mostly he felt something click, the way a puzzle piece clicks when you finally see where it goes.

By last period, the puddle in the freezer had turned back into ice, hard and whole, as good as before. The ash on the tray sat there no matter how long Mason stared at it. He tried dripping water on it, then pressing it between two sheets of paper, as if pressure might help. Nothing. The smoke had gone out the window; the ash stayed ash. He wrote in his notebook: burning is a chemical change, and it cannot turn back into wood. Then, out of curiosity, he toasted a marshmallow over the candle and bit into it while it was still warm.

"It's still sweet," he said, chewing. "Is toasting a chemical change too, or did I just make a nutritious snack?"

Marina snatched the bag of marshmallows. "Not nutritious," she said, and held one over the flame.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
story:
Evan sat on the bench by the duck pond with a folded note in his pocket. He had written it last night, after the fight, and today Arielle was due at the park at ten with Emiliano for their usual Saturday game. The fight had started when Evan knocked Arielle's model sailboat off the shelf at her house and the mast snapped. He hadn't meant to, but he also hadn't helped pick up the pieces, and she had told him to leave.

At five past ten, Arielle and Emiliano came up the gravel path. Arielle was carrying the repaired boat, a small wooden vessel with a new mast, and she set it on the pond edge where the breeze was light. Emiliano read the note when Evan handed it over, because Arielle said she wasn't talking to him yet. "It says, 'I'm sorry if you got upset,'" Emiliano read aloud, squinting at the pencil letters. "That sounds like it's her fault for being upset. Like she shouldn't have been."

Evan looked at the words again. He had thought the "if" made it polite, but now he could see it pointed the regret at Arielle's feelings instead of at what he had done. He took the note back, walked to the trash can by the water fountain, and dropped it in. Then he stood in front of Arielle. "I'm sorry I knocked your boat down, and I'm sorry I didn't help clean it up. That was my fault, not your feelings."

Arielle studied him for a moment. "Emiliano's brother calls those non-apologies," she said. "Sorry if you got upset. It's a thing people do." She crouched and set the boat on the water. The wind pushed it sideways, nearly perpendicular to the shore, and it drifted toward the reeds. Emiliano grabbed a long stick and angled the hull back around.

"We need a compromise," Evan said. "You want it to sail straight out, Emiliano wants to rescue it, and I want to steer." Arielle handed him the string she had tied to the bow as a leash. "You steer, since you broke it. You fix what you break, on the water and off it."

Evan knelt on the flat rock and tugged the string gently. The little boat swung around, caught the wind, and crossed the pond in a clean line toward the far bank, its new mast straight and its sail full. Arielle sat down beside him on the rock, close enough that their elbows touched. "Faster," she said. "Pull it faster, before the ducks get in the way."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron, so almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
story:
Justin lined up twelve marbles on the workbench in his dad's garage: six blue for protons, six green for neutrons, and six tiny beads for electrons. The project sheet from Ms. Santoso said to build a carbon atom, and the marble kit from the hobby store had seemed perfect until he opened it and found the beads.

Dennis leaned against the garage door, spinning a screwdriver between his fingers. "So the blue ones and the beads are the same size in the picture on the box," he said. "Is that right?"

"That's what the box shows." Justin frowned at the box. It had a glossy painting of an atom with fat blue spheres and fat yellow spheres, all the same size, circling a cluster in the middle. He had copied that picture for his sketch, and tomorrow he was supposed to present the model to the class. He picked up a blue marble and a bead and held them side by side. Something felt off, and he could not say what.

He went inside and came back with the science book Ms. Santoso had lent him. He found the page on atomic particles and ran his finger down the column of facts. Then he stopped. He read the line again, out loud. "A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron."

Dennis whistled. He set down the screwdriver. "So the bead should be how small?"

Justin did the arithmetic on a scrap of sandpaper with a pencil stub. "I can't make it that small. If the marble is this size, the electron would basically be dust." He looked at the kit, then at the pile of scrap in the corner of the garage, where his dad, a veteran of twenty years in the machine shop, kept bits of wire and sheet metal. "The box picture is wrong. Almost all of the atom's mass is in the nucleus. The middle part."

"So what do we do?"

Justin tested it. He glued the six blue and six green marbles into a tight clump on a washer, then clipped six short lengths of the thinnest wire he could find. He dabbed glue on the tip of each wire and touched the tip to the head of a pin. Six pins, six wires. When he stuck the wires into a foam ring around the nucleus, the pins were barely visible. "That's more like it," he said. "The pins are the electrons. Tiny, way out here."

Dennis picked up the finished model and turned it in the light. "My brother did the same project three years ago. He used gumballs for everything."

"He got it wrong," Justin said. "My dad would call that building to the drawing instead of building to the part." He wrote a note card to go with the model, then read it once, decided it sounded too fancy, and crossed out the word "eloquent" he had put in the first line. He wrote plainly instead: the nucleus holds nearly all the mass.

At school the next morning, Maxim squinted at the ring of pins. "Where are the electrons?"

"Look closer," Justin said, and held the model up to the window, where the six pinheads caught the light.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A persuasive essay is stronger when it states the best opposing argument fairly and then answers it; this answer is called a rebuttal.
story:
Parker set his hot chocolate down on the cafe table, careful not to slosh it onto the crumpled paper in front of him. The paper had three sentences on it and a crossed-out fourth, and every sentence said the same thing: kids should be allowed to wear beanies in class because the room is cold.

"You've said 'cold' four times," said Asma, leaning over from the next chair. "Also 'freezing,' 'arctic' and 'polar.'"

"The room is like the tundra," Parker said. "On Tuesday I could see my breath near the pencil sharpener. We might as well be doing math on a glacier."

Guillaume stirred his cocoa with a straw he had bent into a spiral. "Mr. Fischer won't even read it, though. He reads one paragraph and says, 'Convince me, Parker.'"

"It does convince."

"It repeats. It's like a song with one note."

Parker glared at the page. Then Asma pulled a folded handout from her backpack, the one Mr. Fischer had given out Friday, and smoothed it flat between the sugar and the napkin holder. Parker read it upside down while pretending not to. It said an essay is stronger when it states the best argument from the other side fairly and then answers it.

"That's backwards," Parker said. "Why would I help the other side?"

"Try it and see," Asma said. "My sister says it's called a rebuttal."

Guillaume grinned. "Do the other side. Be the principal. Cold, strict, allergic to hats."

Parker sat up straight and pinched the bridge of his nose like a man with many important meetings. "Beanies hide earbuds," he said in his sternest voice. "Beanies are rebellious. Students who wear them will start a hat crime wave."

"That's actually his best one," Guillaume admitted. "The earbud thing."

Parker stopped grinning. The earbud thing was good. He took a real sip of chocolate and wrote at the bottom of his draft: Some say beanies hide earbuds, and that is a fair concern. Then he stared at it, straw-tapping, until an idea landed. He added: But earbuds are already banned, so a teacher who sees them can take them, hat or no hat. Beanies insulate heads; they do not block rules.

He read it out loud. Asma nodded slowly, the way she did when a thing finally worked. Guillaume pointed his straw at the paragraph. "It sounds smarter when it admits the other guy has a point. That's weird and I don't like it, but it's true."

"The weird part," said Parker, "is that it's easier to argue against the principal when I say his whole argument out loud first. Like I'm holding it up and turning it around."

"Draft two," Asma said, sliding him a clean napkin. "Five paragraphs this time, and only one 'tundra.'"

"One and a half," said Parker, already writing.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
story:
Leo charged onto the community center basketball court with his whole team buzzing behind him. Today was the tournament final, the one they had circled on the calendar since June. The gym's windows were open, but the air hung thick and sticky, like a wet towel pressed against everyone's face.

By halftime, Leo was dripping. He tugged his soaked shirt away from his chest and stared at the scoreboard, which still showed the game close. That was the strange part. Last weekend had been even hotter, yet he and Theron had sprinted up and down the court all game without feeling wrecked. Today everybody on both teams looked gray and slow, bent over with their hands on their knees. "It's the air," Robyn gasped on the bench. "It feels like a swamp in here."

Leo turned that over while Mr. Çelik, the referee, checked the clock. Something was different, but he could not see it, so he tried to reason it out. In dry weather his sweat vanished from his skin, like magic. Today the sweat just sat there, rolling down his arms in fat drops. He had a theory: sweat must be doing something when it disappeared, something that helped him. If the sweat evaporated fast, maybe he cooled off fast. In this soupy air, his sweat barely evaporated, so maybe he wasn't cooling down at all. He whispered it to Theron. "That actually sounds credible," Theron said, wide-eyed. "You sweat buckets, but you stay boiling."

Mr. Çelik called for a water break right then, and Leo's coach waved everyone toward the fans in the hallway. Leo set a personal objective for the second half: short, careful shifts on the court, plus lots of water. He wasn't going to hibernate on the bench, though, not in the final. He jogged back out, sweat still clinging to his skin like it had nowhere to go, and slapped his hands together. "Let's finish this," he said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
Declan stood in his grandmother's kitchen with a heavy pot and a bag of sugar, because tonight he was making dessert for the whole family. His grandfather had inherited the house along with its ancient stove, whose burners ran hot on the left side no matter what the dial said, so Declan kept the pot on the right and watched the sugar melt from white crystals into a pale gold liquid. His friends Malak and Andrea had come over to help, though mostly they were eating the crackers he had set aside for the cheese course.

"Is this the same browning as the crust on the roast your grandpa made?" Andrea asked, peering into the pot. "Like, is it the same reaction?"

Declan thought about the crackling brown edge on the roast, then about the pot in front of him, which held nothing but sugar and heat. "It can't be the same," he said slowly. "There's a word for this one. Caramelization. It's browning that happens when sugar alone is heated." He frowned. "The roast one has a name too. I saw it in a cookbook at school. The Maillard reaction."

Malak leaned on the counter. "So what's the difference?"

"Sugar alone," Declan repeated, tapping the pot's handle. "Maillard needs amino acids too. Meat has those. Sugar doesn't." He decided to test it. He poured two small pans, one with plain sugar, one with sugar mixed with a splash of milk, and set them side by side over matching flames. If browning needed only sugar, both would turn at the same time. If it needed something more, the milk pan would behave differently.

The plain sugar darkened first, smooth and even. The milk pan browned faster in patches and went foamy in a way the other one never did, and Andrea wrote down the times in her notebook like a lab report. "So they're really two different things," she said.

The twist came at dinner. Declan carried out a caramel sauce so glossy that his grandfather actually set down his fork, and when everyone asked how he had made it, he explained the two pans, the milk, the timing. His grandmother laughed and said the milk pan had browned that way because she had switched the right burner on without telling him, to test whether he was paying attention. Declan looked at his notes, then at the stove, and realized he had been watching the wrong variable the whole time.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we redo the experiment."

"Bring the sauce again," said Malak, already reaching for the spoon.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: StoryCorps is a project in which people record interviews with family members, and with permission the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress.
story:
The train pulled into the station with a long sigh, and Anna stood on her toes to see through the crowd. Her grandmother was coming to stay for a whole week, and Anna had a plan she had been turning over for days. Next to her, her friend Mago gripped the barrier and peered down the platform. "I just want to see a real conductor's hat up close," Margo whispered. "Do you think he'd let me try it on if I asked politely?" Anna said probably not, but Margo could assess the situation herself when the passengers came through. Then the doors opened, and there was Grandma, small and quick, hauling a suitcase painted with faded flowers.

"Your mom says I talk too much," Grandma announced on the drive home. "A whole week of me." Anna, from the back seat, said she hoped so. All week she listened, and she began to notice a pattern: Grandma's best stories came out at night, after the dishes, when the kitchen was warm and nobody rushed her. Stories about the farm, and about the winter a rodent got into the flour bin and her mother screamed so loud the neighbor heard it a field away. Anna started writing the stories down, but her hand couldn't keep up, and she wondered whether there was a way to keep the actual voice, the laugh in the middle of the flour story, not just the words.

On the last night, Anna carried the family tablet to the kitchen table. She had learned about a project at school where people record interviews with family members, and with permission the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress. "It's called StoryCorps," Anna said. "Your stories could go there. Forever. Like a library, but with voices." Grandma was quiet for a moment, her teacup halfway to her lips. "Would anybody be able to hear them?" "Only if you say yes. It's voluntary." Grandma set the cup down. "Then press your button, child. Start with the rodent."

Anna pressed record. The little red light came on, and Grandma leaned forward, hands folded, as if the Library of Congress were sitting right there at the table. "It was February," Grandma began, "and the snow was up to the fence posts."

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Bright screens late at night can delay sleep, because light, especially blue light, signals the brain to hold back the sleep hormone melatonin.
story:
Cooper had been looking forward to his first sleepover at Keaton's house all week, and so far everything was going perfectly: pizza, a fort made of couch cushions, and three hours of funny videos on Keaton's tablet with the screen turned up bright.

At eleven o'clock, Keaton's mom made them put the tablet away and turn out the lights. "Sleep now," she said. "Swim practice is at eight."

They lay in the dark, whispering about the videos, then about nothing, and then not whispering at all. Cooper stared at the ceiling. His body felt tired, but his brain stayed wide awake, like a light left on in an empty room. He rolled over. Keaton rolled over. The clock on the wall ticked past midnight.

"That's it," Cooper whispered. "We watched videos for hours, and now we can't sleep. I hypothesize the screen did something."

"To my eyes?"

"No, to sleep itself. I read that light, especially blue light, signals the brain to hold back the sleep hormone. Melatonin, it's called. It's the thing that makes you sleepy." Cooper sat up. "So here's my idea. We can't see it happening, so let's test it. Tomorrow, no screens after dinner. If we fall asleep fast, the screen was the hidden cause."

"That's plausible," Keaton said. "But what about tonight? Practice is in seven hours."

They tried Cooper's backup plan: face away from the window where the streetlight glowed, breathe slowly, and think about something dim and boring, like a gray rock. It took a long time, but eventually Keaton's breathing went slow and heavy.

The next morning at the pool, both of them yawned through every lap, and the coach made them run an extra set of drills as punishment for sloppy turns.

That night was Saturday, no alarm waiting. After dinner, Keaton put the tablet in a drawer himself. "The mechanism stays out of the bedroom," he said, very seriously, and switched on a small lamp with a warm yellow bulb instead.

Cooper was asleep before the lamp clicked off.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, to show it was not in the original text.
story:
Mr. Dela Cruz had written one word on the board: theme. Matthew stared at it and felt the fatigue of a boy who had read forty pages the night before and understood maybe ten of them. The class novel was about a runaway dog, and everyone kept saying the theme was "dogs are loyal," which sounded like a poster, not an idea.

"Theme is the big invisible thing the whole book is about," Mr. Dela Cruz said, walking between desks. "Prove yours with a quotation. Due at the end of class."

Matthew flipped pages. He found a line he liked: "He never stopped searching, even when the trail went cold." Perfect, except the "he" was the dog, and if he just copied the sentence, it would look like some random man was searching. Princeton leaned over from the next row.

"Just write 'the dog' in there," Princeton whispered.

"That's changing the quote," Matthew whispered back. He tried diagnosing the problem like a math problem: the original words were fixed, but the sentence needed one clarifying word that the author never wrote. Was that against the rules? He couldn't remember. He raised his hand. "Mr. Dela Cruz, what if you need to add a word to a quotation to make it clear?"

"Then in MLA style, square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, to show it was not in the original text," Mr. Dela Cruz said, and kept walking.

Matthew wrote: "[The dog] never stopped searching, even when the trail went cold." He looked at it. The brackets were like little flags saying, this part is mine, not the author's. Honest, somehow.

Then Hiba spun around from the front row, waving her paper. "Wait, Matthew, read page two hundred again. The trail goes cold because the dog stops on purpose. He's not searching anymore. He's found where he belongs."

Matthew turned the pages, his thumb smudging the edge. The dog was lying down at the end, ears up, waiting at a door. He crossed out his whole theme, and at the bottom of the page he wrote: "Sometimes home finds you."

"That works," Hiba said. "Now prove it."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
story:
Lydia sat in the emergency room clutching her right arm, which throbbed with an acute pain every time she forgot and tried to move it. She had fallen off the monkey bars reaching for the fifth rung, and Ocean had run for the teacher while Marylou stayed beside her all the way here, even though the fluorescent lights and the smell of antiseptic made Marylou's nose wrinkle.

While they waited, a boy across the room had his cast taken off. Lydia watched him hold out both arms in front of him, and she saw it: the arm that had been in the cast looked skinnier than the other one, noticeably thinner, like a carrot next to a cucumber.

"That's weird," she whispered. "It looks like it shrank."

"Maybe the cast squished it," Marylou said.

Lydia shook her head, then stopped because shaking made her arm yell at her. "The cast was loose the whole time, I saw. It has to be something else. He couldn't move it for weeks, that's the difference." She turned the idea over. Muscles that never get used, she thought. Maybe they get weak and small when a limb is kept still.

"How would you even test that?" Ocean asked.

"With a ruler." Lydia pointed her chin at the gift shop. "Can you simulate what I measured in science class? Mark a spot on each arm, same place, and measure around it."

Ocean came back with a fabric measuring tape from the cashier, who said her granddaughter used it for sewing. Marylou held the tape while Ocean wrote the numbers on Lydia's paper wristband: left arm twenty-four centimeters, right arm twenty-four centimeters.

"Exactly the same," Lydia said. "So when they cut this cast off in six weeks, if my right arm is thinner, we'll know why. Stillness makes the muscles shrink."

"I'm writing the date in my notebook," Ocean said.

"You're both getting ice cream after this," Marylou promised, and squeezed Lydia's good hand.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: If a price is held above the equilibrium price, sellers offer more than buyers want, and unsold goods pile up as a surplus.
story:
Ethan sat on the wooden bench inside the bank, holding his school project paper so tight that the corners curled. Ms. Watanabe's assignment was due tomorrow morning, and his topic, supply and demand, was still a blank page. His mother was at the teller window, waiting to deposit a check, and the clock above the counter showed 4:42. The bank closed at five, and his mother had promised they would drive straight home to the library afterward, which closed at six.

"You look like a boy carrying a heavy rock," said Ms. Watanabe, the neighbor who also happened to work at this branch. She sat down beside him on her break, and the smell of her coffee mixed with the lemon-scented cleaner the janitor was using on the glass doors. Outside, gray lichen crept up the stone pillar by the entrance, and the sky had the flat look of imminent rain.

"I have to explain why strawberries are cheap in summer and expensive in winter," Ethan said. "I keep writing stuff and crossing it out."

Devon's lemonade stand flashed into his mind from last July. Devon had sold strawberry lemonade for three dollars a cup because strawberries were everywhere then, cheap in every crate at the farm stand. But three dollars was more than anyone wanted to pay, so by sunset Devon had two full jugs left over and dumped them in the sink. The cheap berries hadn't helped, because the price was the problem. "Sellers offered more lemonade than buyers wanted," Ethan said slowly, "and the extra just piled up."

He borrowed a pen from Ms. Watanabe's counter and started writing on the back of his paper. Summer meant loads of strawberries, so sellers had plenty to offer, and prices dropped to where buyers actually bought them all. Winter meant almost none, so prices climbed. He drew two jagged lines, labeled one Supply and one Demand, and marked where they crossed. "The price where those two lines coincide," he said, "that's the price where sellers sell exactly what buyers want."

"I have no idea what that means," Ms. Watanabe said, "but you said it like a man who knows."

"I think I finally do." Ethan looked up at the clock, 4:55, and his mother was waving him toward the door while the first raindrops streaked the glass. He folded the paper once and ran.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The lower a light source is, the longer the cast shadow it makes, so a lamp near the table throws a long shadow and a lamp overhead a short one.
story:
Florence sat at her grandmother's kitchen table, laying siege to the same drawing for the third evening in a row. Her art teacher wanted a shaded sphere by Friday, and Florence's ball of gray looked flat as a pancake no matter how hard she pressed the pencil. "Grandpa," she called toward the living room, "do you have something round I can borrow?" Mr. Santos shuffled in with an orange in one hand and his old desk lamp in the other, because he never brought just one thing. "The lamp emits a clean white light," he said, setting both on the table. "Better than that yellow bulb over your shoulder." He wanted his kitchen table back by Sunday for his card game, and he said so.

Florence propped the orange on a sheet of paper and switched on the lamp. When she held the lamp high, almost over the orange, the shadow on the paper was a small dark puddle. When she lowered the lamp toward the tabletop, the shadow stretched out long and skinny, reaching almost to the edge of the page. She moved it up and down three times to be sure. Low lamp, long shadow. High lamp, short shadow.

She grabbed her phone and called Juan, who was stuck on the same assignment. "Put your lamp near the table," she said. "Mine's practically touching the paper. My cast shadow looks like a footlong fish." There was a clatter on his end, then a pause. "Whoa. Mine was tiny because my lamp's on the top shelf." Jasleen texted a photo a minute later of a shadow so long it ran off her page, and Florence texted back one word: "Lower."

By Friday she had a sphere with a bright highlight on top, soft shading down the side, and a long cast shadow lying across the drawn tabletop. Her teacher circled it in red pen and wrote "consistent light source," and Florence grinned all through lunch.

On Sunday, Mr. Santos dealt cards at the newly cleared table and nodded at the drawing, now taped to the refrigerator beside her grandmother's grocery list. "So," he said, "what do we owe the orange?"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
Livia jogged into the gym with her shoes squeaking on the polished floor, because tonight was the first real practice of the season and she could not wait. The banners on the wall portrayed a hawk swooping down, which was meant to look fierce, but Lacey had drawn a tiny mustache on one hawk last year and it had somehow become permanent. Nobody could get it off.

"Did you hear?" Lacey whispered, tying her shoes. "Zara's been here every single day since September. Even Sundays. She wants to be captain so bad."

Mr. Campbell-Brown blew his whistle and set up the sprint drill, the one with the orange cones. Livia's whole plan for the season was to beat Zara at it, just once. But when they ran, something strange happened. Zara, who had trained more than anyone, was slow. Not a little slow. Slower than Lacey, who had spent most of August eating popcorn at her cousin's lake house.

Livia chewed on the mystery through two drills. Zara worked harder, so Zara should be faster. Unless the working itself was somehow part of the problem. She thought about her old rabbit, who always slept after big runs and came back faster the next day.

At water break, Livia sat down beside her. "Try something for me. Skip the gym tomorrow. The whole day. Watch what happens."

"Skip?" Zara looked at her like she'd suggested skipping gravity. "There's a bake sale to plan, Livia. Being captain is a whole corporation of paperwork. I don't have time to get slower."

"Muscles get stronger during recovery, not during the workout itself," Livia said. "Rest days are part of getting better."

Zara stared, then grinned. "One day. One."

The next practice, Zara flew past every cone like the floor was on fire, and Lacey chased her yelling, "Fine! New captain! But I want to portray the mustache in the yearbook!"

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: The most common kind of hydrogen atom has just one proton and one electron and no neutron at all.
story:
James had been sitting on the garage floor for twenty minutes, staring at the shoebox of painted ping-pong balls Ms. Kim had given him after the science fair meeting. The red ones were protons, the gray ones neutrons, and the tiny blue beads were electrons, meant to hang on bent wire. Aleksander sat across from him, already threading a bead onto a coat hanger. "You start with a big one, right?" Aleksander said. "Like oxygen, sixteen of everything, so it looks impressive."

"I did that last year," James said. He thought about how that model had looked, big and crowded and praised by everybody, and how he had not really understood a single part of it. Building it had felt like camouflage, something impressive to hide behind, and the judges' compliments had been wasted on him. He had decided, in a vain sort of hope that this year would be different, to build the smallest atom instead and actually know it. The problem was the smallest one, hydrogen, was giving him trouble before he even started. He kept reaching for a gray ball out of habit.

"Every atom needs a neutron, doesn't it?" he said, holding up the gray ball. "Something in the middle holding it together." He set it down, picked it up again, then turned to his dad's science almanac on the workbench, the one with the crumpled cover and the page corners that had started to erode from being turned so often. He found the table of elements and ran his finger along the first row. "Hydrogen," he read slowly. "The most common kind has just one proton and one electron." He checked twice, because it seemed impossible. "No neutron at all."

Aleksander leaned over to see for himself. "So the simplest atom in the universe is one red ball and one blue bead," he said. "That's it?"

"That's it," James said. He dropped every gray ball back into the shoebox, hung a single blue bead on one loop of wire, and set it orbiting the lone red ping-pong ball on the workbench.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
Rosalie found Jeanne in aisle three, holding a bright orange bottle up to the light like it might contain jewels. "VeloCharge," Jeanne read. "Six ninety-nine. I drank one before the time trial and I dropped four seconds, so obviously it works." A fine settlement of orange grit sat at the bottom of the bottle, which Rosalie felt said something about the contents, though she didn't say what.

Rosalie turned the label around. The ingredients list ran to vitamins, caffeine, and something called "proprietary focus blend," which sounded like a way of not telling you anything. She read the back twice. "It doesn't say it makes you faster. It says 'supports energy.'" She could exclude almost everything on the list as a possible cause of speed, since she'd eaten three of the vitamins that morning in cereal form and remained slow. "I drank one too," she said. "I felt like a cheetah. Nothing changed, but I felt like one." That was the part that bothered her.

Mr. Ho, at the counter, had been listening the way he listened to everything, which was completely and without appearing to. He set down a box of bandages. "We sell sugar pills here, you know. Homeopathic ones. Some people swear by them." He straightened his name tag. "There's a name for it. The placebo effect." He rang up the customer in front of them, a man buying cough drops and a lottery ticket, and added nothing further, because Mr. Ho believed in letting a sentence stand there until someone picked it up.

Rosalie picked it up. That night she looked up the words on her mother's ancient computer, and by morning she had a plan, an empty VeloCharge bottle, and a pitcher of water. The water she dyed pale orange with two drops from the food coloring set, since Jeanne would otherwise notice, and Jeanne noticing would ruin everything. She could not exclude the possibility that Jeanne would also notice the cap was slightly loose, but she decided to risk it.

At the track, Jeanne drank the whole bottle, grimaced at the grit settlement Rosalie had faked with half a teaspoon of Tang, and ran the practice 400 in her second-best time ever. "See!" she gasped at the finish line, waving the empty bottle over her head. "Six ninety-nine well spent." Rosalie considered mentioning that the entire cost had been tap water. Jeanne was, apparently, immune to that sort of information. "Same time tomorrow?" Rosalie asked, and tucked the bottle into her bag for refilling.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: An oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius.
story:
Alexis stood in front of Ms. Bennett's muffin stall at the farmers' market, holding a basket of blueberries like it was a bomb about to go off. "I'm going to bake these into muffins," she announced. "All by myself. From start to finish."

"Even the oven part?" said Sonny, who was next to her, eating a cinnamon bun the size of his face.

"Even the oven part," said Alexis. Her grandmother had always said she'd be ready when she could do it alone, and Alexis had a plan to prove it this very afternoon.

Anne-Sophie jogged up with a printed recipe in her hand. "Found it online. It's from an American website, so watch out."

They walked home, and Alexis laid everything out on the counter like a general arranging a battle. Flour, sugar, eggs, oil, and a bowl big enough to bathe a small cat in. The recipe said to preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Alexis turned the dial and stopped cold. Her oven only showed numbers up to 250, and there was no 350 anywhere.

"Oh no," she said. "This oven is broken. Or American. Or both."

Sonny leaned over her shoulder. "Maybe you're supposed to turn it past the end and it loops around, like a video game?"

Alexis was tempted. Last summer, when the three of them had tried to make a cake at Anne-Sophie's cottage, they had cranked the oven as hot as it would go because hotter meant faster, obviously. The result had been a black disc that Sonny tried to classify as either a Frisbee or a fossil, and that Anne-Sophie's dog wouldn't even sniff. Alexis did not want a repeat of the Charcoal Cake Incident.

"Wait," said Anne-Sophie, squinting at the bottom of the printout. "There's a little line here. It says 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. Our ovens just speak Celsius. It's like the recipe is talking in a different language."

Alexis looked at the dial again. Between 150 and 200, clear as anything, sat 175. She set the dial there and heard the oven click and begin to hum. "So the recipe wasn't wrong and the oven isn't broken," she said. "They just count differently."

While the oven heated, they mixed the batter. Alexis cracked an egg one-handed, missed, and had to fish out a piece of shell, which Sonny called "the monarchy of Shell Island," ruling over the bowl until she dethroned it with a spoon. She folded in the blueberries, filled the muffin cups, and slid the tray in at a confident diagonal, which Sonny claimed was for luck.

Twenty minutes later, the kitchen smelled like a bakery. Alexis pulled out twelve golden muffins, and the three of them stood around the cooling rack, guarding it like it held treasure.

"See?" said Alexis, splitting one open, steam curling up into the light. "One hundred seventy-five. I told you I could do it."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
At dinner, Camille pushed her rice around her plate and finally said it out loud. "The comic convention is Saturday, and I'm fourteen dollars short for a ticket. I have until Friday night, because tickets close then."

Her father looked up from his noodles. "You still have that box of contemporary graphic novels you said you'd outgrown?"

"Thirty-one of them," Camille said. "I was going to sell them at the garage sale on Saturday, but that's too late. The sale is Saturday morning and tickets close Friday night."

Clemence, who was eating with them because her parents were working late, set down her fork. "Then contract with the neighbourhood," she said. "You know, make a deal. Knock on doors tonight and sell them one by one. Ms. Hussain on the corner is always saying she wants to read what kids are reading."

Camille's motive was simple, and she admitted it: she wanted that ticket so badly her stomach hurt. But she had a problem she couldn't see the answer to. What price? Too high, and nobody would buy. Too low, and even if all thirty-one sold, she might not raise fourteen dollars.
