She tried five dollars a book. At Clemence's building, two people bought, then a boy complained, and three people walked away shaking their heads. Too many wanted it at a lower price, she noticed, and too few at a higher one. So she dropped to three dollars, and at the corner store, a woman with a baby bought four. By Friday evening, the box felt light, the paper smell of old pages on her hands, and she counted twenty-two dollars. One book was left.

"The last one didn't sell until I hit two dollars," Camille told her mother at the dinner table, sliding the crumpled bills into a zippered pouch. "Clemence said the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price. I found it by accident."

"Well," her mother said, "accidents count."

Camille grinned and zipped the pouch shut. "Tomorrow, I'm buying my ticket."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
story:
The lights went out at Grandma's house just after supper, and the whole kitchen dropped into blue shadow. Ava heard her grandmother's slippers scuffing toward the pantry, where the candles lived on the second shelf beside the birthday napkins.

"Wait," Ava said. "Don't light those."

Grandma's hand was already on the shelf. "We've used candles since I was your age, sweetheart."

Ava stood still, thinking. Last year Mr. Oyelaran had drilled a fire-safety unit into her sixth-grade class until everyone could recite it, and something about it had stuck. She could picture the handout, even the little citation at the bottom naming the safety agency that had published it. "He said safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut," she said slowly, "because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house." She had drawn a flame on her copy of that page, she remembered now, and he had circled it in red.

"Then where are the flashlights?" Grandma asked.

"Kitchen drawer. The one by the sink." Ava had noticed two of them there that morning when she was hunting for the potato peeler. She felt her way along the counter, bumped her hip on a chair, and pulled the drawer open. Her fingers closed around cold metal. She clicked the first one, and nothing happened, so she twisted its base and it blazed bright across the table. The second one worked too, and Grandma laughed and sat down.

"You're a resilient girl, finding those in the dark," Grandma said.

Ava handed her one of the lights. "Jad's house lost power for two whole days last winter. His family kept a flashlight in every room so they could sustain the outage without stumbling around." She swept her beam across the pantry shelf, where the candles waited, then closed the door on them.

Grandma set her flashlight upright on the table like a little lantern. "Well then," she said, "go get the cards."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: The prime meridian, at 0 degrees longitude, was set through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, by an international conference held in Washington, D.C., in 1884.
story:
Oliver pressed his nose against the window of Carter's Travel Agency, where a frail old globe spun slowly on a brass stand behind the glass. Ms. Pritchard had put a sign in the window that said "Map Day: Come Learn Your Coordinates." He had walked past the shop twice already that morning, telling himself he would go in tomorrow instead. Last week he had told Zarah that London was at 90 degrees north, and she had laughed so hard she had to sit down on the gym floor. He still wasn't sure he wanted to be corrected again, but he pushed the door open anyway.

Inside, the shop smelled of old paper. Zarah was already there, standing at the counter with a peach nectar in a paper cup, arguing with Ms. Pritchard about a poster of London. "I need the exact location of the city," Zarah said. "For our project. Oliver promised he could find it, and I'm not letting him wreck my grade." Her grandmother had been born in London, and Zarah wanted to find the street on a map before she asked for a trip there next summer.

Oliver found London on the globe's bumpy surface and looked for the numbers printed along the edges. The horizontal lines counted up toward the pole, and the vertical ones counted from a thick line marked zero. He turned the globe slowly. "So London is at about 51 degrees north," he said, "and zero degrees longitude, because it sits right on that thick line." He tested it against Paris and then Madrid, checking whether the numbers grew bigger or smaller as he moved east and west, and they did, both ways, like a rule the whole world had agreed to.

"That's the prime meridian," Zarah said, pointing at the thick line. "I stood on it. On my trip last spring. There's a real line on the ground at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, and tourists stand on it with one foot on each side." She sipped her nectar. "I asked the guide why the world's zero was there, of all places, and he said it wasn't London's idea at all. An international conference decided it, in Washington, D.C., in 1884. They just picked the observatory."

Oliver stared at the globe. A city in England had been chosen as zero for the whole planet by a meeting in America, an ocean away. He wondered whether the people at that conference had argued about it, and whether some of them had wanted their own cities instead. There was no way to know from where he stood, holding a peach nectar Ms. Pritchard handed him without a word.

"Write it down before you forget," Ms. Pritchard said, sliding a pencil across the counter. Oliver copied the numbers onto the back of the project sheet: 51 degrees north, 0 degrees longitude, Greenwich, 1884. Then he gave the globe one more spin and watched London come around again, right on the line.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Facing a person with hearing loss and speaking clearly helps them understand more than shouting does.
story:
Nora had been counting down to Grandma's visit for two whole weeks, and now the suitcase was in the hallway and Grandma was actually here, standing in the kitchen smelling of lavender and rain. There was only one problem, and Nora discovered it at breakfast on the very first morning.

"GRANDMA, DO YOU WANT TOAST?" Nora shouted from the counter, thirteen feet away. Grandma squinted and tilted her head. "Has the post come?" she asked. Nora shouted again, louder, and Grandma guessed wrong a second time, then a third. By the time the toast was cold, Nora felt like she'd run a race. Her friend Luke had a grandfather who couldn't hear well, and Luke had told her once that shouting just made it worse, though Nora hadn't believed a word of it. Shouting was louder. Loud was more. That seemed plausible the way two plus two equals four.

But the evidence at breakfast pointed somewhere else. Nora thought about it while she buttered a new slice of toast. Maybe the problem wasn't loudness at all. Grandma watched mouths when people spoke; she leaned in; she turned her whole body toward whoever was talking. That was a pattern, like a clue. Nora made a quick diagnosis, the way scientists do, and designed a test. She walked over to the table, stood where Grandma could see her face, and said clearly, not loudly, "Do you want jam?"

"Raspberry, please," said Grandma instantly, and then, to Nora's total shock, "You know, your mother shouts at me from the other room and I catch maybe one word in ten. Face me and speak clearly, and I understand far more." Nora almost dropped the jam jar. She had guessed right on her first try, which hardly ever happened.

She ran the experiment all week. She announced dinner plans from two feet away instead of from the stairs, and Grandma laughed at both her jokes instead of just the second one. When Jackson came over to build the cardboard castle for the school project, Nora caught him yelling a question from the dining room and physically steered him around the table until he was looking right at Grandma. "Try it this way," she whispered. Jackson, face to face with her, asked about the trip to the lighthouse. Grandma answered the whole question, and Jackson's eyes went wide.

"You're a genius," he said.

On the last night, Grandma stood in the doorway with her coat already on. From three feet away, looking straight at her, Nora said clearly, "Come back soon."

"Watch me," said Grandma, and tapped the side of her nose.

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: Mayo Clinic advises against cleaning a cut with hydrogen peroxide or iodine, because both can irritate the wound.
story:
Zachary was sitting in the corner of Ridgeline Savings and Loan, waiting for his mother to finish signing papers, when the coin machine jammed. Mr. Vogel, the branch manager, reached in to clear it, and the metal edge caught his thumb. A thin red line opened up across it, and he shook his hand and said a word he immediately apologized for.

"Are you okay?" Zachary asked, already halfway across the lobby. Evelynn and Inara, who had come with him from school, trailed behind.

"Just a cut," said Mr. Vogel. He nodded toward the counter. "First aid kit's under the teller station. Would you grab it?"

Zachary opened the white box and found gauze, tape, butterfly strips, and a brown bottle labeled iodine, plus a smaller one labeled hydrogen peroxide. He reached for the peroxide first, because everyone knew the fizzing bottle was the one for cuts. That was practically a rule of the universe.

But taped to the inside of the lid was a laminated card, a first-aid guide from the Mayo Clinic. He read the cleaning section twice, because it seemed to say the opposite of the universe.

"It says not to use these," he said slowly. "It says don't clean a cut with hydrogen peroxide or iodine, because both can irritate the wound."

"Iodine?" said Inara, leaning over his shoulder. "My grandma swears by iodine. She thinks everything else is toxic."

"Grandma also thinks wifi is a parasite that lives in the walls," Evelynn said.

Inara squinted at the card, then at the bottles. "Huh. Maybe the fizzing isn't actually helping. Maybe it's just... fizzing."

"Like a magic trick," Zachary said. "Looks like it's doing something."

"Would somebody bring the kit or shall I bleed on the deposits?" Mr. Vogel called.

Zachary snapped the bottles back into their loops, took the gauze and tape and the card, and carried them over. "We're rinsing it with water," he announced. "Fresh instructions." He held up the card. "Doctor if it's deep, gaping, or won't stop bleeding. Yours is just a line, so you're probably fine."

Mr. Vogel held out his thumb, and Zachary wrapped the gauze around it, then around again to replicate the first loop exactly, and tore the tape with his teeth.

"That's the neatest bandage I've ever seen on this thumb," Mr. Vogel said. "Ever consider a career in banking?"

Zachary peeled the backing off a butterfly strip, smoothed it down across the cut, and said, "Hold still. I'm not done."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
The X-ray tech slid the film onto the light board, and Kate forgot all about her throbbing arm. Her bones glowed white against a gray blur that she guessed was her skin, like a ghost hand drawn in chalk. "Thea's going to think this is so cool," she said. Her mom was filling out forms at the desk, so the only person near the exam room door was Mr. Choi, her neighbor, who had driven them when the coach called from the gym.

"Coach said you supervise the climbers all day, and I still managed to fall off the wall," Kate said, feeling foolish. Mr. Choi waved that away and leaned closer to the light board with her.

"I heard the doctor tell your mom it's a clean break," he said. "You'll get a cast."

Kate stared at the film. She had assumed X-rays worked like photographs, but a photograph showed skin perfectly, and here her skin was barely visible while the bones burned white. She thought about the museum gift shop where she'd once bought a counterfeit fossil, a fake with a plastic skeleton glued inside real rock. You could tell it was fake by shining a strong light through it; the plastic showed up darker than the stone. Her arm was doing the opposite of that. Something in her bones was soaking up the X-rays, the way a wall soaks up a flashlight beam, while her skin let them pass right through. "The calcium," she said slowly. "The calcium in my bones absorbs more of the X-rays than the softer stuff around them. That's why they show up white and my skin barely shows at all."

Mr. Choi smiled, and just then the doctor came in, so Kate decided to test her idea on someone who would actually know. "Can I ask something?" she said. "Is it the calcium? That's why the bones are white?"

The doctor looked at the film, then at her, clearly pleased. "That's exactly right. The calcium in your bones absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them, so the bones come out white."

"Like a laser pointer stopped by a wall but shining straight through a window," Kate said.

"Close enough," the doctor said, and started unwrapping the roll of cast material. "Pick a color."

Kate pointed with her good arm at the bright purple on the shelf. "That one. And can I keep the X-ray? I want to show Thea and Tori what calcium looks like when it wins."

"You'll have to beat them to the signature line," the doctor said, holding out a marker. "Who's first?"

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United States, a bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president.
story:
Alyssa sat in the third row of the town hall with her notebook open on her knees. The room smelled like coffee and folding chairs, and the overhead lights gave the wooden stage a strange luminous glow. She had come because her class assignment was to ask a real question about government, and Imane had dared her to actually speak into the microphone instead of just writing the question down.

The panel was talking about a new bike-path bill that had been in the news. Alyssa had read that the House had passed one version and the Senate had passed another, and she could not figure out which one would become the law. She raised her hand, and when the moderator called on her, she stood up so fast her chair squeaked. "There are two versions of the bill," she said. "Which one wins?"

A man in the front row, Mr. Zhang, who ran the garden store near her school, turned around. "Neither one wins yet," he said. "The House version has to pass the Senate too, exactly the same, word for word. A bill has to pass both the House and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president."

Alyssa wrote that down, underlining it twice. So it was not a race between the two versions at all. She had been sorting the bills into a category called "winners" and a category called "losers," but that was the wrong way to think about it. The two versions had to match first, like two copies of the same recipe. She tried to paraphrase it in her own words so she would remember. "So the House bill and the Senate bill have to become one bill, the same in every word, and then it goes to the president to sign."

"Exactly," Mr. Zhang said, and the moderator nodded.

After the meeting, Markus from her class caught her by the door. "Did you actually talk into the microphone?" he asked. "I heard you from the back."

"It wasn't that scary," Alyssa said, which was not quite true. She tore out the notebook page, folded it, and put it in her back pocket. "I'm going to read it to the class tomorrow."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: In the United States, falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged 65 and older.
story:
Piper stood in the middle of the guest room with a rolled-up rug in her arms and a question in her head. Grandma arrived in two hours, and Mom had handed her the rug without a word, pointing at the hallway. Piper carried it to the garage, then went back and stared at the pale rectangle it left on the floor. Why that rug? The doormat stayed. The bathroom rug stayed. She walked the whole house, counting: every rug by the stairs, gone; every flat mat in a corner, still there.

She found Mom wrestling the guest room curtain rod. "Grandma can step over a rug," Piper said. "She's not that old." Mom shook her head. "Grandma's sixty-eight, and in the United States, falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged sixty-five and older." Piper repeated the words silently. Not car crashes, not illness. Falls. She had never once thought about a rug as something dangerous.

Outside in the backyard, Leland and Keegan were stringing a banner between the fence posts, and the smell of the hamburgers Dad was grilling drifted across the grass. "We need to check the yard too," Piper told them. "Grandma will want to sit out here." She tested her idea the only way she could think of: she filled a watering can almost full, like a person who couldn't recover balance quickly, and walked every path Grandma might take. The loose flagstone near the tomato pots wobbled under her sneakers. The garden hose, coiled across the walk, caught her toe. "That would do it," she said, and dragged the hose flat against the fence.

Keegan tested the flagstone himself, jumping on it twice. "It rocks like a seesaw," he reported. Piper pried it up and packed sand underneath until it sat solid, then stepped on it, stepped off, stepped on again. Leland held the banner higher so it wouldn't brush anyone's head going through the gate. "You're kind of nurturing this whole yard," he said, and Piper laughed, because that was exactly what it felt like, tending every sharp corner and wobbly stone until the place was safe to land on.

At dinner that first night, Grandma mentioned she'd had a dizzy spell last month. "The doctor said it was an inner ear thing, not anything serious," she added, waving her fork. "A diagnosis, finally. I was starting to worry." Piper set down her water glass and watched Grandma walk to the patio door, step over the threshold, and come back without a single wobble. The path held. It would hold all week.

The last evening, Grandma sat in the lawn chair under the banner, which sagged now in a buoyant, lopsided way that made everyone laugh. She looked around the yard, at the flat hose, the steady flagstone, the clear walk. "How did everything get so tidy?" she asked. Piper shrugged, but she was already wondering whether the flagstone by the school gate rocked too, and whether anyone had ever tested it the way she did. "Grandma," she said, "tomorrow, can we go look at a sidewalk together?"

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: The voice comes from two vocal folds in the larynx that vibrate as air passes between them; tightening them raises the pitch.
story:
Amelia stood on Grandma's porch with her phone propped against a flowerpot, waiting for the choir call to start. In two weeks the middle school chorus would sing at the spring concert, and Mr. Rodríguez had split them into two parts. Amelia had the melody, the part that came naturally. Suri had the harmony, the part that wandered off somewhere lower and, in Amelia's opinion, seemed designed to drag her along with it.

The problem had shown up at Thursday's rehearsal. Every time Suri's section slid into their notes, Amelia's voice followed them down like a dog following a scent. Mr. Rodríguez stopped the piano and said, "Amelia, you're merging. Hold your line." She tried again and merged again. That was why she was at Grandma's house on a Saturday, because Grandma had a piano in the front room and nobody to complain about the noise.

Suri arrived on her bike ten minutes later with a folder of sheet music and a granola bar for each of them. They stood at the piano, and Suri sang her part alone while Amelia listened without singing, tapping the beat on the piano lid. Then they tried together. Amelia followed her down within four bars.

"It's like my ears take over," Amelia said. "I hear you and I just go."

"Your ears aren't the problem," Grandma said, coming through with a watering can. She set it down and pointed at her own throat. "It's these two little vocal folds in your larynx, right here. They vibrate when air passes between them. You tighten them, the pitch goes up. You loosen them, it goes down."

Amelia put her fingers on her throat and hummed a low note. She could feel a buzz, faint but real, like a phone set to vibrate. She hummed higher and the buzz seemed to quicken under her fingers. So that was what was happening every time she slid after Suri: her folds were loosening, dropping her pitch, and it all happened out of sight inside her neck. She couldn't watch it, but she could feel it and, more importantly, she could control it.

"Sing your part," she told Suri. "I'm going to hold my fingers here and keep my pitch up no matter what."

Suri sang. Amelia pressed lightly on her throat, kept the folds tightened on her own note, and held. Her ears pulled at her, but her fingers reported the truth: steady buzz, steady pitch. When they finished the phrase, Suri stared at her.

"You stayed," Suri said. "Eight whole bars."

"Mr. Rodríguez will be so pleased he might make an extravagant speech about it," Amelia said, and Grandma laughed from the doorway. They ran it again, and this time Amelia let her hands hang at her sides and held the line anyway.

"Monday," Suri said, snapping her folder shut, "you contribute the melody, I contribute the harmony, and nobody merges with anybody."

Amelia touched her throat one last time and hummed.

fact: Mandarin has separate words for older and younger siblings: "gēge" means older brother and "dìdi" means younger brother.
story:
Ariana sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her notebook open to a page that read, in careful pencil, "My Family in Mandarin." Tomorrow she had to record herself describing her whole family in full sentences, and every sentence so far sounded like a robot reading a grocery list. Wǒ yǒu yī gè māma. Wǒ yǒu yī gè bàba. She said it out loud and wrinkled her nose. Something was missing, and she couldn't see what.

Then she remembered the confusing part. Her flashcards had two words where English had one. She flipped through the stack until she found them. One card said gēge. The other said dìdi. Why would a language need two words for "brother"? She turned the cards over and over, as if the answer might be hiding on the cardboard itself. She was skeptical of her own guess, because it seemed almost too strange: the words cared about order of birth, not just about having a brother at all.

She needed a test case, so she grabbed her tablet and typed a message to Paxton, who was in her Mandarin class and, more importantly, was a twin.

"Question for science," she wrote. "Was your brother born before you or after you? Exact minutes please."

The reply came fast. "After. Ten minutes after. Why?"

Ariana sat back on her heels. Ten minutes. That was shorter than a TV commercial break, and yet in Mandarin it split the word for brother into two. She typed back, "In Mandarin gēge means older brother and dìdi means younger brother. So what does that make YOU?"

The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again. "Wait. He's only older than me by TEN MINUTES. How is he my gēge? That's like winning a race by one step."

"But he did win," Ariana wrote. "By ten minutes. The language doesn't care about the margin."

For a long moment nothing came back, and Ariana wondered if she'd pushed too hard. Paxton had complained all year about being the "younger twin," and Ariana could almost feel the old resentment coming through the screen, the kind that builds up over years of being handed the smaller piece of cake. Then the reply arrived.

"Okay. Fine. He's my gēge. I'm not happy about it, but it's true. I'll say it in class tomorrow and everything."

Ariana flopped onto her back and laughed at the ceiling. She tried her sentences again, this time with the new words tucked in like puzzle pieces snapping into place. Wǒ yǒu yī gè mèi mei. Wǒ yǒu yī gēge. The robot voice was gone. She could see it now, the pattern hiding inside the language, and it made her wonder what other secrets were waiting in the rest of the flashcards. She reached for the stack, flipped to the next section, and started to read.
